content: 1. A study conducted in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, evaluated the cost-effectiveness of a smoke alarm giveaway program aimed at injury prevention. The findings were published in the journal Injury Prevention in 2001, volume 7, issue 4, pages 276–281. 2. Jutkowitz et al. analyzed the cost-effectiveness of a home-based intervention designed to assist functionally vulnerable older adults in aging in place. Their research was published in the Journal of Aging Research in 2012, article ID 680265. 3. Salkeld and colleagues assessed the cost-effectiveness of a home hazard reduction program aimed at reducing falls among older individuals. This study was published in the Australia & New Zealand Journal of Public Health in 2000, volume 24, issue 3, pages 265–271. 4. The World Health Organization (WHO) published comprehensive housing and health guidelines, emphasizing the importance of safe and accessible living environments. These guidelines are referenced under WHO publication number 142363. 5. Church et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of various fall prevention interventions for older Australians living in the community. Their findings appeared in the Australia & New Zealand Journal of Public Health in 2012, volume 36, issue 3, pages 241–248. 6. Frick et al. examined the cost-effectiveness of fall prevention programs that specifically target the reduction of fall-related hip fractures in older adults. This research was published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society in 2010, volume 58, issue 1, pages 136–141. 7. Ling et al. conducted a cost-benefit analysis of preventing falls among the elderly through environmental modifications in homes in Hana, Maui. Their findings were published in the Hawaii Medical Journal in 2008, volume 67, issue 3, pages 65–68. 8. Kochera analyzed the incidence, costs, and potential savings associated with home modifications to prevent falls among older adults. This report was published by the AARP Public Policy Institute in Washington, DC, in 2002. 9. The WHO introduced the International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health in 2002, providing a standardized framework for understanding and addressing disability and health-related issues globally. 10. The WHO's World Report on Disability (2011) highlighted the global prevalence of disability and the need for inclusive policies and practices to improve the quality of life for individuals with disabilities. 11. The United Nations' World Population Ageing 2015 report provided a detailed analysis of the demographic trends and challenges associated with an aging global population. 12. The Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) provided comments on the draft text of the United Nations' Ad Hoc Committee's convention on the rights and dignity of persons with disabilities in 2004. 13. The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities was adopted by the United Nations in 2006, establishing international standards for the protection and promotion of the rights of individuals with disabilities. 14. Saville-Smith and Saville explored practical approaches to encouraging industry adoption of accessible housing designs in New Zealand. Their report was prepared for the New Zealand Ministry of Business, Innovation, and Employment in 2012. 15. Ubani et al. investigated the accessibility and housing needs of paraplegics in Enugu City, Nigeria. Their findings were published in the Civil and Environmental Research journal in 2013, volume 3, issue 1, pages 17–25. 16. Smith et al. examined the implications of aging and disability for the housing industry and housing policy in the United States. Their research appeared in the Journal of the American Planning Association in 2008, volume 74, issue 3, pages 289–306. 17. Close et al. conducted the Prevention of Falls in the Elderly Trial (PROFET), a randomized controlled trial, to evaluate fall prevention strategies. The results were published in The Lancet in 1999, volume 353, issue 9147, pages 93–97. 18. Whiteford discussed occupational deprivation as a global challenge in the new millennium. This analysis was published in the British Journal of Occupational Therapy in 2000, volume 63, issue 5, pages 200–204. 19. Stanley et al. analyzed the implications of population aging, disability, and housing accessibility for sub-national areas in the United States. Their findings were published in Housing Studies in 2012, volume 27, issue 2, pages 252–266. 20. Gitlin et al. identified factors associated with the quality of life for individuals with dementia living at home, focusing on the role of the home environment, caregivers, and patient characteristics. This study was published in the American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry in 2014, volume 22, issue 6, pages 587–597. 21. Petersson et al. evaluated the impact of home modification services on the ability of people aging with disabilities to perform everyday activities. Their findings were published in the Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine in 2008, volume 40, issue 4, pages 253–260. 22. Gitlin et al. reported on the effects of an in-home occupational and physical therapy intervention in reducing mortality among functionally vulnerable older adults. Preliminary findings were published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society in 2006, volume 54, issue 6, pages 950–955. 23. Stineman et al. conducted a population-based study on home accessibility features and their impact on activities of daily living, with clinical and policy implications. This research was published in Disability & Rehabilitation in 2007, volume 29, issue 15, pages 1165–1175. 24. Brunnström et al. examined the effects of lighting adaptations on the quality of life for individuals with low vision. Their findings were published in Ophthalmic & Physiological Optics in 2004, volume 24, issue 4, pages 274–280. 25. Fänge and Iwarsson explored changes in housing accessibility and usability during the housing adaptation process. Their study was published in Occupational Therapy International in 2005, volume 12, issue 1, pages 44–59. 26. Gitlin discussed theoretical, measurement, design, and implementation issues in testing home modification interventions. This analysis was published in the Annual Review of Gerontology & Geriatrics in 1998, volume 18, issue 1, pages 190–246. 27. Edgren et al. evaluated the effects of a home-based physical rehabilitation program on physical disability following hip fractures. Their randomized controlled trial was published in the Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 28. Tongsiri et al. assessed the modification of homes for individuals with physical disabilities in Thailand. Their findings were published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2017, volume 95, issue 2, pages 140–145. 29. Slaug et al. analyzed the short-term costs and long-term gains of improved housing accessibility for older adults in Sweden and Germany. Their research was published in the International Journal of Environmental Research & Public Health in 2017, volume 14, issue 9. 30. Tchalla et al. evaluated the efficacy of simple home-based technologies combined with a monitoring assistive center in reducing falls among frail elderly populations. The results of the Esoppe study were published in the Archives of Gerontology & Geriatrics in 2012, volume 55, issue 3, pages 683–689.
